blocks.text: Propositional logic gives a precise way to combine true or false statements using operators like AND, OR, and NOT, and it is the exact same boolean logic underlying every conditional statement, filtering operation, and decision boundary throughout programming and machine learning.

blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together

blocks.text: 1. Propositions: Statements That Are True or False
A proposition is a statement that is either true or false, never both and never neither. "It is raining" is a proposition, while a question or a command is not, since neither has a truth value.

code.content:
is_raining = True
is_sunny = False
print(is_raining, is_sunny)

blocks.text: This binary, true-or-false nature is exactly what makes propositional logic so directly translatable into computer code, where every boolean variable is either True or False, nothing in between.

code.content:
# not a proposition: a question has no truth value
# "Is it raining?" cannot be assigned True or False directly

blocks.text: 2. The AND Operator
AND combines two propositions into one that is true only when both original propositions are true.

code.content:
print(True and True)     # True
print(True and False)    # False
print(False and False)   # False

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A loan application might require both a good credit score AND sufficient income, if either condition fails, the combined AND result is False, and the application is rejected.

blocks.text: 3. The OR Operator
OR combines two propositions into one that is true when at least one of the original propositions is true.

code.content:
print(True or False)    # True
print(False or False)   # False

blocks.text: This inclusive definition, true when either or both are true, is the standard mathematical meaning throughout logic and programming, distinct from the sometimes exclusive meaning of or in casual English.
4. The NOT Operator
NOT flips a single proposition true to false or false to true.

code.content:
print(not True)    # False
print(not False)   # True

blocks.text: NOT is the only unary operator covered in this lesson, acting on a single proposition, while AND, OR, and implication each combine two.
5. Truth Tables
A truth table lists every possible combination of true and false inputs alongside the resulting output, giving a complete, exhaustive definition of a logical operator.
A truth table with n input propositions always has exactly 2 to the power n rows, covering every possible combination of true and false values.

blocks.title: Why 2 to the n
blocks.content: Two propositions give 4 rows, three propositions give 8 rows, since each added proposition doubles the number of true or false combinations that must be checked.

blocks.text: 6. Implication: If Then Statements

Implication, written A implies B, is false only in the single case where A is true but B is false, in every other case it is considered true, including when A itself is false, a result that often surprises newcomers.
This unusual true-when-A-is-false behavior is called vacuous truth, the statement makes no claim at all about B whenever its condition A never actually holds.

code.content:
rains = True
bring_umbrella = False
# "if rains then bring_umbrella" is False here, the one case implication forbids
is_valid = (not rains) or bring_umbrella
print(is_valid)

blocks.text: 7. Combining Multiple Operators
Complex logical expressions combine AND, OR, and NOT together, following the same operator precedence rules as arithmetic, with parentheses used to make the intended grouping explicit.

code.content:
age = 25
has_license = True
can_drive_alone = age >= 18 and has_license
print(can_drive_alone)

blocks.text: Just as in arithmetic, NOT is applied before AND, which is applied before OR, by default, though parentheses always override this default ordering explicitly.

blocks.title: Reading tip
blocks.content: When in doubt about precedence, add explicit parentheses, a slightly longer expression that always evaluates unambiguously beats a shorter one that depends on memorized rules.

blocks.text: 8. Predicate Logic: Quantifiers

Predicate logic extends propositional logic with quantifiers, for all, meaning a statement holds for every element in a set, and there exists, meaning at least one element in a set satisfies the statement, letting logical claims be made about entire collections rather than single fixed statements.

code.content:
numbers = [2, 4, 6, 8]
all_even = all(n % 2 == 0 for n in numbers)   # for all: are every one of them even
any_even = any(n % 2 == 0 for n in numbers)   # there exists: is at least one even
print(all_even, any_even)

blocks.text: The for all and there exists quantifiers are usually written using the symbols an upside down A and a backwards E in formal mathematical notation, though plain English or code equivalents work just as well for practical purposes.
The all and any builtin functions in Python are a direct, practical implementation of the for all and there exists quantifiers, applied to any iterable collection of boolean conditions.
9. Boolean Logic in Conditional Code

Every if statement in any programming language is fundamentally evaluating a proposition, true or false, and branching execution based on the result, making boolean logic the literal foundation of conditional program behavior.
Nested if-elif-else chains are really just a structured way of testing a sequence of propositions in order, executing the first block whose condition evaluates to True.

blocks.title: Short-circuit evaluation
blocks.content: Python stops evaluating an AND expression as soon as it hits a False, and stops an OR expression as soon as it hits a True, since the final result is already determined, this is called short-circuit evaluation.

blocks.text: 10. Boolean Masks in Data Filtering

Filtering a dataset with a condition like age greater than 18 produces a boolean mask, an array of True and False values, one per row, that pandas and numpy use directly to select only the rows where the condition holds.

code.content:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"age": [15, 22, 30, 17]})
mask = df["age"] >= 18
print(df[mask])   # only rows where the boolean mask is True

blocks.text: Combining multiple boolean masks with logical AND and OR operators, using the ampersand and pipe symbols in pandas specifically, lets complex, multi-condition filters be built directly from simpler individual conditions.
Every row of a boolean mask lines up positionally with the corresponding row of the original dataframe, which is exactly what allows it to be used directly as a row selector.
11. Logic in Decision Trees

Every split in a decision tree is a boolean condition, a feature value compared against a threshold, and the tree structure itself is a nested chain of AND-combined logical conditions leading to each final leaf prediction.

Reading a full decision tree path from root to leaf is equivalent to reading one long AND-combined logical statement describing exactly which conditions a data point satisfied to reach that particular prediction.
12. XOR: Exclusive Or
XOR, exclusive or, is true when exactly one of two propositions is true, but false when both are true or both are false, distinct from ordinary OR which allows both to be true.
XOR shows up directly in classic machine learning history as the simplest example of a pattern a single linear classifier cannot separate, motivating the development of multi-layer neural networks.

code.content:
# XOR via the caret operator on booleans
print(True ^ False)   # True
print(True ^ True)    # False

blocks.text: 13. A Worked Example
Evaluate the compound proposition (A OR B) AND (NOT C) for A = True, B = False, C = True.

code.content:
A, B, C = True, False, True
result = (A or B) and (not C)
print(result)   # False, since NOT C is False

blocks.text: Working through a compound expression like this one step by step, innermost parentheses first, is the most reliable way to avoid an operator precedence mistake.

blocks.title: Step by step
blocks.content: A or B evaluates to True first, since A is True, then not C evaluates to False, since C is True, and finally True and False evaluates to the final answer, False.

blocks.text: 14. Common Mistakes

items: Confusing implication direction, A implies B is not the same statement as B implies A, they can have different truth values.
Forgetting operator precedence, writing an ambiguous expression without parentheses that gets evaluated differently than intended.
Misreading a false implication, forgetting that A implies B is considered true whenever A itself is false, regardless of B.
Confusing the logical AND and OR with everyday English usage, where or sometimes means exclusive or, only one, rather than the inclusive or logic normally uses.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is treating a predicate logic quantifier claim as proven by checking only one or a few examples, a for all claim requires every single case to hold, not just the ones that were checked.
15. Practice: Build a Truth Table
Build the truth table for the expression NOT (A AND B) by hand, then verify it in code against every combination of True and False for A and B.
Comparing this hand built truth table against the code output directly confirms whether the logical intuition and the formal definition agree.
Extending this same practice pattern to expressions with three propositions instead of two is a natural next exercise once the two-proposition case feels automatic.
Key Takeaway

Propositional logic combines true or false statements using AND, OR, and NOT, fully defined by truth tables, while predicate logic extends this with quantifiers to make claims about entire collections. This exact boolean framework underlies every conditional statement, data filter, and decision tree split used throughout applied programming and machine learning.

This lesson closes out the Discrete Mathematics module, having covered sets, relations, functions, graphs, and counting, logic ties the whole module together as the formal reasoning framework every other topic ultimately depends on to state precise, checkable claims.

XOR, from the newly added section, is a small but historically significant example of the limits of simple linear models, directly motivating the more expressive architectures covered throughout the rest of an applied AI curriculum.

Short-circuit evaluation, covered in the conditional code section, is also a useful performance detail, placing the cheaper or more likely to fail condition first in an AND chain can skip unnecessary work entirely.
